catalog_quote: Accent. Accent usually falls on the final syllable of a word, but forms with certain suffixes retain accent on the stem rather than the suffix. In any event, accent is predictable only from word or morphological boundaries, and therefore it is indicated in the phonemic (rather than morphophonemic) transcription used here.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Strand quotation is verbatim in the held at the stated place (line 251, 'Accent' bullet), and the Halfmann 2024 supporting passage is verbatim in the held txt. (2) Deciding source: a brief first-hand online phonology sketch (2011, rev. 2024) by the leading Nuristani fieldworker, for the Sanu dialect. Against Glottolog (only Morgenstierne 1929/1934 sketches + Trumpp 1866) and the sources Halfmann cites, nothing better exists: no reference grammar, phonology paper or instrumental study of Ashkun is on record. (3) I downloaded the two open primary alternatives. Grjunberg 1999: 127 (Jazyki mira, Wama-based) independently states the same rule — stress mostly word-final, exceptions in certain verb forms, tone distinctions noted but unclear — which confirms 'default final, morphologically conditioned exceptions'. Morgenstierne 1929: 202, 217 gives no rule, c

sources.quote: p.202 §22: 'I had the impression that Ashk. may have a musical accent as well as a stress accent; but I dare not assert anything about this difficult question, as I heard the language spoken for a short time only. ... I noticed a musical accent, generally accompanying the stress, but being in some cases independent of it. ... It is of course impossible to draw any conclusions from these imperfect and scanty observations.' fn.1: 'ˈ before the syllable denotes stress, ´ over the vowel denotes high pitch.' p.217: 'The terminational vowel and the accentuation are uncertain' (future-tense verb form
